```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(

```

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(MultiStateTMLE)
```

We will in this vignette use the following example: how many deaths would be
prevented by a drug that makes an illness less likely?

# The Data

`illness_death` is a simulated dataset of a trial of 200 patients who may fall
ill and may die, with follow-up subject to censoring. The `illness` can occur at
most once and raises the hazard of death. Patients were randomised to
`treatment` (`1`) or placebo (`0`), and patients with a higher baseline
`biomarker` are more likely to fall ill.

```{r}
#| label: data

head(illness_death)
```

Each row is an event: the patient `id`, the `time` of the event, which `event`
it was, and the baseline covariates. A patient who dies without falling ill has
one row, like patient 3, while one who falls ill and then dies has two, like
patient 2:

```{r}
#| label: data-example

illness_death[illness_death$id %in% c(2, 3), ]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Simulated data"}
This is the format `simevent::simulate_events()` returns, so data simulated with
[simevent](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/simevent) can be used directly.
`illness_death` itself was simulated with simevent, which lets us check the
estimates against the truth below.
:::

# Fitting the Hazards

The first step is to model the hazard of each event. `fit_initial()` takes one
formula per event, with the event on the left and the covariates of its hazard
on the right. Using another event's name as a covariate gives its number of
events so far, so `death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness` lets the illness
change the death hazard:

```{r}
#| label: fit-initial

models <- list(
  hazard_model(illness ~ biomarker + treatment, limit = 1),
  death ~ biomarker + treatment + illness,
  censoring ~ biomarker
)
fit <- fit_initial(illness_death, models = models, tau = 1)
fit
```

By default each hazard is a Cox model, so the death hazard is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
    \lambda_{\text{death}}(t) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\big(
     & \beta_1 \, \text{biomarker} + \beta_2 \, \text{treatment} \\
     & + \beta_3 \, \text{illness}(t) \big),
  \end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{illness}(t)$ is 1 once the patient has fallen ill. `tau = 1` is the
time horizon: everything below concerns what happens by time 1.

::: {.callout-note title="Hazard models"}
Every event in the data needs a model, censoring included. A plain formula is
short for `hazard_model(formula)`, which also takes `limit`, the most events a
patient can have (here one illness), and `at_risk`, a condition such as
`~ illness == 0` for when patients are at risk.
:::

# Halving the Illness

Without any intervention, `tmle_estimate()` estimates the risk of death by
`tau`, given by `risk()`:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-observed

observed <- tmle_estimate(fit, risk(death))
observed
```

Now suppose the drug halves the hazard of the illness. `scale_intensity()`
multiplies a hazard by a factor $\alpha$, and the estimate is the risk of death
had the illness hazard been $\alpha \lambda_{\text{illness}}(t)$:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-halved

halved <- tmle_estimate(fit, risk(death), scale_intensity(illness = 0.5))
halved
```

Halving the illness lowers the risk of death from `{r} round(coef(observed), 3)`
to `{r} round(coef(halved), 3)`. The other hazards, death given illness
included, are left as they are.

`coef()` and `confint()` extract the estimate and its confidence interval:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-ci

coef(halved)
confint(halved, level = 0.9)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Reading the output"}
The standard error comes from the efficient influence curve, so no bootstrap is
needed. The last line gives the estimate from the initial fit alone, which TMLE
then *targets*: it updates the fitted hazards until the estimate solves the
efficient influence curve equation. This removes the first-order bias of the
initial fit, so the confidence interval is valid even with flexible hazard
models.

Here no targeting was needed: the Cox fits already solve the equation to within
the stopping criterion, $\text{se} / \log n$, so the estimate is the initial
estimate. With 200 patients this is common, since the remaining bias is small
next to the standard error. With larger samples, or more flexible initial fits,
expect one or more targeting steps.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Other interventions"}
A factor of `0` removes the illness, and one above `1` increases it. The factor
can also be a formula in `time`, the baseline covariates and the events so far,
for example a drug that only works early, or only for patients with
`biomarker > 0`:

```{r}
#| label: tmle-time-varying

coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  scale_intensity(illness = ~ ifelse(time < 0.5, 0.5, 1))
))
coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  scale_intensity(illness = ~ ifelse(biomarker > 0, 0.5, 1))
))
```

Several events can be scaled at once, as in
`scale_intensity(illness = 0.5, death = 0.8)`.
:::

# From Hazards to Risks

"Halve the hazard" is hard to interpret: what does it mean for how many patients
fall ill? `intervention_curve()` answers this for a grid of factors $\alpha$,
estimating both the risk of the illness, the *exposure*, and the risk of death:

```{r}
#| label: intervention-curve

curve <- intervention_curve(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  exposure = risk(illness),
  alpha = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)
)
curve
```

Plotting one against the other shows how the risk of death responds to the risk
of illness:

```{r}
#| label: intervention-plot
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Estimated risk of death plotted against the estimated risk of illness
#|   across interventions on the illness hazard, with 95% confidence intervals.
#|   The risk of death increases with the risk of illness.

ce <- curve$estimate

plot(
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$estimate,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  las = 1,
  bty = "l",
  ylim = range(ce$lower, ce$upper),
  xlab = "Risk of illness by time 1",
  ylab = "Risk of death by time 1"
)
arrows(
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$lower,
  ce$exposure_estimate,
  ce$upper,
  angle = 90,
  code = 3,
  length = 0.04
)
```

Removing the illness altogether (the leftmost point) lowers the risk of death by
about `{r} round(100 * (coef(observed) - ce$estimate[1]))` percentage points.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Checking against the truth"}
`illness_death` was simulated from the model below, so simevent can tell us the
true risks under each intervention, by simulating many patients without
censoring and with the illness hazard scaled by `intervene`:

```{r}
#| label: truth
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("simevent", quietly = TRUE)

library(simevent)

true_model <- sim_model(
  biomarker = sim_covariate(function(N) rnorm(N)),
  treatment = sim_covariate(function(N) rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)),
  illness = sim_process("transient", limit = 1, eta = 0.7, nu = 1),
  death = sim_process("terminal", eta = 0.3, nu = 1),
  censoring = sim_process("censoring", eta = 0.1, nu = 1),
  effects = list(
    sim_effect(illness ~ biomarker + treatment, coef = c(0.5, -1)),
    sim_effect(death ~ illness + treatment, coef = c(1.2, -0.3))
  )
)

true_risks <- function(intervene) {
  sim <- simulate_events(
    true_model,
    n = 1e5,
    cens = 0,
    intervene = intervene,
    seed = 1
  )
  risks <- event_risk(sim, true_model, c("illness", "death"), tau = 1)
  setNames(risks$risk, risks$process)
}

check <- ce[, c("alpha", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
check$truth <- sapply(
  check$alpha,
  function(alpha) true_risks(list(illness = alpha))["death"]
)
check
```

Every interval covers the truth, and the estimates follow the true curve
closely, removing the illness included.
:::

# Calibrating the Drug

Often the question is about risks directly: what if the drug prevented 20% of
illnesses? `calibrate()` finds the factor $\alpha$ for which the risk of illness
reaches a given value, and estimates the risk of death under it:

```{r}
#| label: calibrate

calibrated <- tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  risk(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
)
calibrated
```

The first table gives the calibrated $\alpha$ and the risk of illness $\theta$
it reaches, 80% of the observed
`{r} round(ce$exposure_estimate[ce$alpha == 1], 3)`. The second gives the risk
of death under it.

::: {.callout-note title="Calibration rules"}
The target risk of illness can be given in three ways:

- `level(theta)`: the risk is `theta`.
- `absolute_change(delta)`: the risk is `delta` plus its observed value.
- `relative_change(rho)`: the risk is `rho` times its observed value.

Because $\alpha$ is itself estimated, the standard error `se` accounts for its
uncertainty. `se_crude` is the standard error if $\alpha$ were known.
:::

`years_lost()` gives the expected years of life lost before `tau` instead of the
risk, and can be used wherever `risk()` can:

```{r}
#| label: calibrate-years-lost

coef(tmle_estimate(
  fit,
  years_lost(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(0.8))
))
```

# Explaining a Treatment Effect

So far `treatment` has only been a covariate. Suppose instead we want its effect
on death, and how much of it is because treated patients fall ill less often.
The calibrated intervention above answers this: give patients the treatment, but
calibrate their risk of illness to what it would have been on placebo. This
splits the total effect into two contrasts:

- *mediated*: treatment versus the calibrated intervention, the part that goes
  through the illness, and
- *calibrated*: the calibrated intervention versus placebo, the rest.

`treatment_model` tells `fit_initial()` how treatment was assigned, so that
estimates can be made with everyone treated or everyone on placebo:

```{r}
#| label: trial-fit

trial_fit <- fit_initial(
  illness_death,
  models = models,
  tau = 1,
  treatment_model = treatment ~ biomarker
)
```

`a` sets everyone's treatment, and `reference_a = 0` calibrates the risk of
illness to that under placebo:

```{r}
#| label: trial-arms

treated <- tmle_estimate(trial_fit, risk(death), a = 1)
placebo <- tmle_estimate(trial_fit, risk(death), a = 0)
treated_calibrated <- tmle_estimate(
  trial_fit,
  risk(death),
  calibrate(risk(illness), relative_change(1), reference_a = 0),
  a = 1
)
treated_calibrated
```

To give treated patients the risk of illness they would have had on placebo,
their illness hazard must be multiplied by about
`{r} round(treated_calibrated$calibration$estimate[1], 1)`.
`calibrated_contrasts()` then combines the three fits:

```{r}
#| label: trial-contrasts

contrasts <- calibrated_contrasts(treated, placebo, treated_calibrated)
contrasts
```

Treatment lowers the risk of death by
`{r} round(-100 * contrasts$estimate$estimate[1])` percentage points, of which
`{r} round(-100 * contrasts$estimate$estimate[2])` go through the illness.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Checking against the truth"}
With `true_model` from before, simevent gives the true contrasts too: simulate
each arm without censoring, and for the calibrated arm search for the factor on
the illness hazard that matches the risk of illness on placebo:

```{r}
#| label: trial-truth
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("simevent", quietly = TRUE)

placebo_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 0))
treatment_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1))
true_alpha <- uniroot(
  function(alpha) {
    calibrated <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1, illness = alpha))
    calibrated["illness"] - placebo_risks["illness"]
  },
  interval = c(1, 5),
  tol = 0.01
)$root
calibrated_risks <- true_risks(list(treatment = 1, illness = true_alpha))

check <- contrasts$estimate[, c("contrast", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
check$truth <- c(
  treatment_risks["death"] - placebo_risks["death"],
  treatment_risks["death"] - calibrated_risks["death"],
  calibrated_risks["death"] - placebo_risks["death"]
)
check
```

Every interval covers the truth. With 200 patients the contrasts are estimated
less precisely than the risks, since each compares two arms of about 100.
:::

# Where Next

- `risk()` and `years_lost()` take several events at once, as in
  `risk(death, illness)`, count only events in some states, as in
  `risk(death, when = ~ illness == 0)`, and for recurrent events give the
  expected number of events, or the risk of a first one with
  `only_first = TRUE`. See `?"target-parameters"`.
- To simulate event history data, and the truth under interventions, see
  [simevent](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/simevent).
